33:2.text: I know that ye are Abraham’s seed; but ye seek to kill me, because my word hath no place in you.

provenance.other: “hath no place in” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 8:37. The idiom of a word or spirit having no place in a person is unattested elsewhere in the Bible.
provenance.significance: The source is one of the sharpest exchanges in the Fourth Gospel, and Nephi has taken the accusation and changed its subject. In John, what has no place is Christ's word, and the hearers are Abraham's seed who nevertheless seek to kill him; in 2 Nephi 33:2, what has no place is the Holy Spirit, and the hearers are those who cast away what is written. Recover John 8 and the charge Nephi is making against the rejectors of his book is the charge Jesus made against the children of Abraham — that descent from the right father is no protection when the word finds no room. Which is precisely the argument Nephi will make in his own person six verses later, at 33:8: “I have charity for the Jew; I say Jew, because I mean them from whence I came.”

33:2.note: Four words, one KJV verse, and the construction is reproduced intact including the preposition and the pronoun object. The single change — Christ's word becomes the Holy Spirit — is the change the colophon needs, because Nephi's subject is not his own words' rejection but the Spirit's. The 1830 spelling “nought” at the end of the verse, which 1920 modernized to “naught”, keeps the KJV's own orthography.

33:3.text: Pilate answered, What I have written I have written.

provenance.other: “what I have written” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, John 19:22, and the doubled perfect — the clause repeated verbatim as its own predicate — occurs nowhere else in the Bible in any form.
provenance.significance: This is the find of the chapter and it is uncomfortable. Nephi's assertion of his own authority as a writer — “I, Nephi, have written what I have written” — is, word for word, Pilate's refusal to amend the title on the cross. The chief priests ask him to write that the man SAID he was King of the Jews; Pilate declines, and the sentence is the Gospel's image of a text that stands whatever its readers think of it. That is exactly what Nephi wants to claim, and the fact that the one biblical voice claiming it is the man who condemned Christ is not something the borrowing acknowledges. Metalepsis cuts both ways here: recover the context and the colophon's confidence acquires an author it would not have chosen. The task brief was right that colophon formulae often look biblical and are not; this one is, and the surrounding formulae in the same verse are not.

33:3.note: Six words in a doubled construction with a single biblical home. Confidence is high rather than certain only because the sentence is so natural a thing for any writer to say that independent coinage cannot be formally excluded — but the KJV has no other instance, and the Book of Mormon is a text that quotes John constantly, including three chapters earlier at 2 Nephi 31:4 and 31:10. The rest of 33:3 is not biblical in the same way: “I esteem it as of great worth” and “I cry unto my God in faith” have no identifiable source, and Nephi's own earlier colophons at 1 Nephi 6 and Jacob 7 were adjudicated without one.

33:3.text: I am weary with my groaning; all the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears.

provenance.other: “water my couch” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 6:6, and it is the Bible's only instance of tears as the verb of watering a place of sleep. Job 16:20's “mine eye poureth out tears unto God” and Jeremiah 9:1's “fountain of tears” share the grief and not the image.
provenance.significance: The transferred epithet is the whole of it. Psalm 6:6 waters a couch; 2 Nephi 33:3 waters a pillow, and the substitution is the sort a writer makes who has the image by heart and not the verse in front of him. The Psalm is the first of the penitential psalms and its speaker weeps for himself under God's chastening; Nephi's weeping is intercessory, “for them by day … because of them”. The borrowed image has been turned outward, which is the same turn the chapter makes at 33:7-9 with charity.

33:3.note: “Mine eyes water my pillow by night, because of them.” The verb, the object-as-place, and the nocturnal setting are all Psalm 6:6's; Nephi supplies the eyes as the grammatical subject, which the Psalm does not, and swaps couch for pillow. Note that the KJV's “all the night” becomes “by night”, paired with Nephi's “continually for them by day” — the Psalm's single nocturnal image has been opened into a day-and-night antithesis that Psalm 6 does not have. Below any reasonable quotation threshold and catalogued as an allusion accordingly.

33:4.text: Quenched the violence of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, out of weakness were made strong, waxed valiant in fight, turned to flight the armies of the aliens.

provenance.other: “out of weakness were made strong” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Hebrews 11:34. 2 Corinthians 12:9-10 is the passage a reader expects here — “my strength is made perfect in weakness”, “when I am weak, then am I strong” — but neither verse contains the phrase, and neither has weakness made strong as a completed passive.
provenance.significance: The Book of Mormon has been reading Hebrews 11 since its second chapter. 1 Nephi 2 built the departure from Jerusalem out of Hebrews 11:8-9, 1 Nephi 4:2 built the Red Sea exhortation out of Hebrews 11:29, and here, at the last page Nephi writes, the promise for his own book comes from Hebrews 11:34. The catalogue's note at 1 Nephi 4:2 proposed that the Book of Mormon works through Hebrews 11 in order and uses it as an index to the Old Testament. This verse is the strongest confirmation of that reading available, because it is the furthest point in the chapter and the furthest point in Nephi's writing, and because the borrowing is no longer about an Israelite hero at all — it is about a manuscript. Hebrews 11's roll of those made strong out of weakness ends, in Nephi's hands, with a book.

33:4.note: “The things which I have written in weakness, will be made strong unto them.” The KJV's exact collocation, with weakness as the source-state and strength as the passive outcome, and with Nephi's own writing put in the place Hebrews gives to Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthae. Note the 1830 “things”, which 1920 changed to “words” — the first edition's noun is the vaguer one, and the later editors' correction moves the sentence toward a claim about the text and away from a claim about its contents. The verse's closing “endure to the end, which is life eternal” is Nephi's own formula from 2 Nephi 31:15 and is registered there, not here.

33:6.text: For great is thy mercy toward me: and thou hast delivered my soul from the lowest hell.

provenance.route: Psalm 86:13 + Psalm 49:15 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.other: “delivered my soul from the lowest hell” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Psalm 86:13, and it is the Bible's only first-person statement of a soul brought out of hell. “Redeem my soul” is the Psalter's other half of the idea — Psalm 49:15, “God will redeem my soul from the power of the grave” — and the Book of Mormon has the verb of the second with the object of the first.
provenance.significance: “He hath redeemed my soul from hell” is a conflation of the Psalter's two statements about a soul retrieved from below, taking Psalm 49:15's redeeming and Psalm 86:13's hell. Neither psalm says both. The interest is that this is the same kind of seam as 2 Nephi 31:15, where Matthew 10:22's protasis was welded to Matthew 24:13's apodosis: two verses of one book, joined at the point where the memory holds the more idiomatic half of each. Two such conflations in three chapters is a small but real datum about how this text handles its sources.

33:6.note: Recorded at moderate because no single KJV verse supplies the clause and the reconstruction is therefore an argument rather than an identification. What makes it worth having is the pairing: the Psalter contains exactly two verses about a soul brought up from the place of the dead, and 2 Nephi 33:6 contains exactly the elements of both and nothing else. The three-fold “I glory” that opens the verse has no biblical model — Paul glories in tribulations, in infirmities, in the cross, but never in a series of three, and never in plainness.
33:6.whyNot: A conflation argued from two verses neither of which is reproduced. A reader may reasonably hold that “redeemed my soul from hell” is ordinary devotional English of the period requiring no source at all, and the phrase does recur in the Book of Mormon.

33:7.text: But why dost thou judge thy brother? or why dost thou set at nought thy brother? for we shall all stand before the judgment seat of Christ.

provenance.other: “judgment seat of Christ” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Romans 14:10 and 2 Corinthians 5:10. Nothing in Nephi's wording separates them; Romans is named because it also carries “set at nought”, the idiom the chapter used five verses earlier at 33:2, and the two verses stand a page apart in Nephi's text.
provenance.significance: The tribunal is Paul's and so is the reason for mentioning it. Romans 14:10 invokes the judgment seat to stop Christians despising one another; 2 Nephi 33:7-9 invokes it to declare charity for three groups in turn — my people, the Jew, the Gentiles — which is the same argument put positively. And the pairing of a judgment seat with charity is not accidental in a chapter that has been standing on 1 Corinthians 13 since 2 Nephi 31:13: Nephi, who took the tongue of angels from a passage that says it is nothing without charity, closes by claiming the charity.

33:7.note: A shared technical phrase and a shared argument, without a reproduced run, so this is an echo at moderate. “That I shall meet many souls spotless at his judgment seat” — “spotless” is not a KJV word at all, which is worth saying plainly, since a reader will expect 1 Peter 1:19's “without blemish and without spot” or 2 Peter 3:14's “without spot” behind it and the wording is not there. Only the tribunal is biblical.
33:7.whyNot: Four words of a fixed New Testament phrase and no way to choose between its two occurrences. The verse's other distinctive terms — charity, spotless — either belong to Nephi or belong to a chapter of Paul already linked elsewhere.

33:10.text: Look unto me, and be ye saved, all the ends of the earth: for I am God, and there is none else.

provenance.other: “all the ends of the earth” occurs in seven KJV verses and is on its own too common to identify a source. What narrows it is the grammar: Isaiah 45:22 is the only one of the seven in which the ends of the earth are ADDRESSED — a vocative followed by an imperative of turning and being saved. The other six speak about them in the third person.
provenance.significance: Nephi's peroration reproduces the one biblical construction that matches what he is doing. “All ye ends of the earth, hearken unto these words, and believe in Christ” is Isaiah 45:22's vocative plus imperative plus promise of salvation, with looking replaced by believing and the exclusive claim (“I am God, and there is none else”) transposed into the exclusive claim already made at 2 Nephi 31:21 out of Acts 4:12. The address recurs at 33:13, where it is joined to the house of Israel — so the last two summonses in Nephi's book are both Isaiah 45:22's, and both are aimed past his own people.

33:10.note: The link is to a construction rather than to a run of words, hence conceptual and moderate. It is worth a row because the vocative is genuinely restricted — one of seven — and because the salvation clause travels with it in both places. Note that Nephi's argument here is circular and openly so (“if ye believe not in these words, believe in Christ. And if ye shall believe in Christ, ye will believe in these words”), which is a structure Isaiah 45 does not supply; only the address does.
33:10.whyNot: The phrase itself is common and the identification rests on syntax. A reader who takes “all ye ends of the earth” as a general biblicism rather than a citation of Isaiah 45:22 has not made an error, only a different judgment.

33:11.text: And then shall appear the sign of the Son of man in heaven: and then shall all the tribes of the earth mourn, and they shall see the Son of man coming in the clouds of heaven with power and great glory.

provenance.other: “with power and great glory” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 24:30 and Luke 21:27, and both are the same saying in the same discourse. Mark 13:26 reads “with great power and glory”, which is a different word order and is therefore excluded by the Book of Mormon's phrasing.
provenance.significance: Mark is ruled out and Matthew and Luke are not separable, which is a small mediation result but a real one: the Book of Mormon has the Matthew-Luke form of the phrase and not Mark's. What Nephi does with it is the interesting part. In all three Gospels the power and great glory attend the Son of man's coming; in 2 Nephi 33:11 they attend a demonstration about a document — “Christ will shew unto you, with power and great glory, that they are his words”. The parousia has been made the occasion of a textual attestation, with Nephi and his reader standing face to face at the bar. It is the boldest claim in the colophon and it is made in borrowed words.

33:11.note: Four words in sequence, in the word order that separates Matthew and Luke from Mark. The 1830 “Christ will shew unto you” again preserves the KJV spelling that 1920 modernized to “show” — the third such case in these three chapters, after 31:9 and 32:5. “Face to face” in the same verse is a KJV idiom but a widely distributed one, and 1 Corinthians 13:12 is not proposed as a source for it.

33:13.text: For this is he that was spoken of by the prophet Esaias, saying, The voice of one crying in the wilderness, Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make his paths straight.

provenance.route: Isaiah 40:3 via Matthew 3:3 → KJV → Book of Mormon, fused with Isaiah 29:4
provenance.mt: Isaiah 40:3 reads “The voice of him that crieth in the wilderness”.
provenance.other: “the voice of one crying” occurs in exactly four KJV verses — Matthew 3:3, Mark 1:3, Luke 3:4, John 1:23 — and in none of them is it the Old Testament. Isaiah 40:3, which all four quote, reads “the voice of him that crieth”. The mediation is therefore decided by the pronoun, and mediation-check.py returns it as the one decisive divergence.
provenance.significance: Nephi's last self-description is a fusion of two Isaiah passages, and only one of them reaches him through Isaiah. “The voice of one crying” is the New Testament's form of Isaiah 40:3, not Isaiah's own — every Gospel has “one crying”, the prophet has “him that crieth” — so the phrase enters by way of John the Baptist. “From the dust” is Isaiah 29:4, which Nephi has already expounded twice in this book, at 26:16 (“their speech shall be low out of the dust”) and in the expansion of Isaiah 29 at chapter 27. The result is that Nephi signs off as the Baptist speaking from the grave: the forerunner's title, applied to a dead man's book, out of the dust of the buried record. And the frame closes exactly — 2 Nephi 31:4, the first verse of this final sequence, is about “that Prophet which should baptize”; 2 Nephi 33:13, the last but two, takes that prophet's own words for Nephi himself.

33:13.note: Five words verbatim in the NT form, with Isaiah's own wording available and not used. This is the mediation finding of the three chapters and it is decidable on a single pronoun, in the manner of the sixteen such rows the 1 Nephi pilot produced. The fusion with Isaiah 29:4 is not a second borrowing but Nephi's own established idiom, argued at 26:16 and at 27, and pointed to here rather than restated.

33:14.text: But he answered and said, It is written, Man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God.

provenance.route: Deuteronomy 8:3 and/or Matthew 4:4 → KJV → Book of Mormon
provenance.mt: Deuteronomy 8:3 reads “every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of the LORD”.
provenance.other: “proceedeth out of the mouth” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Deuteronomy 8:3 and Matthew 4:4, which are the same saying: Matthew quotes Deuteronomy in the wilderness temptation. They differ in one word, the divine name — the LORD in Deuteronomy, God in Matthew.
provenance.significance: This is the mediation case in these three chapters that will not resolve, and it is worth saying why rather than guessing. The test is normally the divine name, and here the name has been replaced: 2 Nephi 33:14 reads “out of the mouth of the Lamb of God”, which is neither the LORD nor God but John's title, already used in this sequence at 31:4 and 31:5. mediation-check.py reports no decisive divergence, correctly. The word “God” is present, which is Matthew's noun and not Deuteronomy's, but it is present as part of a Johannine title that Nephi would have written whichever source he had in view, so it decides nothing. Recorded as uncertain and flagged in the report.

33:14.note: Four words of a saying that exists in the KJV in two forms, with the one discriminating word overwritten by the Book of Mormon's own christology. The echo is worth recording because 33:14 is building a hierarchy of words — the words of the Jews, my words, the words of the Lamb — and the third term is described in the Bible's one formula for words that come from God's mouth. Note that Deuteronomy 8:1 is separately linked at 2 Nephi 32:6, two verses above this one in its own chapter, which is a mild argument for Deuteronomy 8 being in view here as well; it is not strong enough to settle the mediation and it is not treated as if it were.
33:14.whyNot: Four words, no decisive divergence between the two candidates, and the phrase is common enough in devotional English that a source need not be posited at all. Kept because the mediation question it raises is itself the finding.

33:15.text: And I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt bind on earth shall be bound in heaven: and whatsoever thou shalt loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.

provenance.other: “bind on earth” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Matthew 16:19 and Matthew 18:18, and they are the same formula. The KJV never uses “seal” in this sense at all — sealing in the KJV is the closing of a book (Isaiah 29:11, Daniel 12:4) or the marking of the elect (Revelation 7:3), never the ratification of an earthly act in heaven.
provenance.significance: If the echo stands, the interest is entirely in the substituted verb. Nephi's “what I seal on earth, shall be brought against you at the judgment bar” has the shape of Matthew's binding formula — an indefinite relative, an act on earth, a consequence above — with a verb the KJV does not supply for it. And the verb Nephi chooses is the one Isaiah 29:11 uses for a sealed book, which this book has expounded at 2 Nephi 27:7-11. The formula for ecclesiastical authority and the image of the sealed record have been welded together in the last sentence Nephi writes.

33:15.note: Recorded at low because the argument is about a construction whose one distinctive word has been replaced, which is close to the definition of an undemonstrable link. It earns the row rather than an exclusion because 33:15 is the final verse of Nephi's writing and the reader who feels Matthew 16:19 behind it deserves to be told what the catalogue made of that feeling: the shape is Matthew's, the vocabulary is not, and the sealing comes from Isaiah 29 by way of this book's own chapter 27. The closing “thus hath the Lord commanded me, and I must obey” has no biblical source — Acts 5:29's “We ought to obey God rather than men” is the verse a reader will reach for and it shares only the verb.
33:15.whyNot: The one word that would make the link decidable is absent, and it is absent by substitution rather than by paraphrase. Two words of contact (“on earth”, plus an indefinite relative) cannot carry a source, and the sealing image is fully accounted for within the Book of Mormon itself.
